title: Johnny Ludlow
description: Published from 1867 in the Argosy and collected from 1874: the finest English series of domestic mystery stories, told by a Worcestershire schoolboy.
plot_or_argument: Johnny Ludlow, a boy of a Worcestershire county family, recounts the mysteries and disasters of his neighbourhood — a missing will, a poisoning, a ghost, a wrongful accusation, a lost child — in a series of quietly narrated stories in which the ordinary life of the English county is disturbed by crime and the supernatural.
principal_characters: Johnny Ludlow; Mrs Todhetley; Mr Todhetley; the Squire; the schoolmaster; the villagers of Dyke Manor
historical_context: 1867-79: the English county family, the Worcestershire countryside, the periodical market of the Argosy, and the vogue of the domestic detective story.
literary_significance: Johnny Ludlow is the best English series of domestic mystery stories of the century and the finest thing Wood wrote: its quiet narration, its county setting and its use of a boy's point of view made it a model for the English village mystery, and it is the point at which the sensation novel turns into the detective story.

title: Lord Oakburn's Daughters
description: Published in 1864 and one of Wood's strongest sensation novels: two sisters, a stolen inheritance and a murder in a country house.
plot_or_argument: The two daughters of Lord Oakburn are left poor by their father's death and cheated of their inheritance by a scheming relative; the novel follows their courtships, a murder in the grounds of the family house, and the slow discovery of the truth, in a story of class, money and female vulnerability.
historical_context: 1864: the serial market of the 1860s, the English county family in decline, the law of inheritance, and the sensation vogue after East Lynne.
literary_significance: Lord Oakburn's Daughters shows Wood's sensation method at its most effective: its combination of the vulnerable sisters, the stolen inheritance and the country-house murder made it a favourite of the 1860s, and it is a fine example of the domestic crime novel that preceded the detective story.

title: The Bab Ballads
description: Published in 1869 and the finest English comic verse of the period after Lear: sixty ballads written for Fun and illustrated by the author.
plot_or_argument: The ballads present a gallery of comic unfortunates — the captain of the Pinafore-type ship, the bishop who is eaten by a boa constrictor, the lady who is carried off by a gorilla, the baby farmer, the thwarted lover — each in a narrative that proceeds by impeccable rhyme and impossible logic to a shocking or absurd conclusion.
historical_context: 1861-69: the comic magazine Fun, the burlesque theatre of the 1860s, the Victorian nursery and the illustrated comic book.
literary_significance: The Bab Ballads are the masterpiece of English comic verse between Lear and Gilbert's own operas: their perfect technique and their savage absurdity made them a permanent classic, and they are the direct source of the Savoy opera plots and of the modern English comic poem.

title: H.M.S. Pinafore; or, The Lass That Loved a Sailor
description: First performed in 1878 and the first great Savoy opera: a captain's daughter loves a common sailor, and a forgotten baby-swap makes everything right.
plot_or_argument: Josephine Corcoran, the captain's daughter, loves the sailor Ralph Rackstraw but refuses him because of the difference in class; the bumboat woman Little Buttercup reveals that she had years ago swapped the babies of Captain Corcoran and Ralph, so that the captain is really the lowly sailor and Ralph the gentleman, and the lovers are united while the class order is restored in reverse.
principal_characters: Captain Corcoran; Josephine Corcoran; Ralph Rackstraw; Little Buttercup; Sir Joseph Porter; Dick Deadeye
historical_context: 1878: the Royal Navy of the 1870s, the English class system, the American copyright wars of the 1870s, and the commercial theatre of Richard D'Oyly Carte.
literary_significance: H.M.S. Pinafore was the first English opera to conquer America and the founding work of the Savoy operas: its satire of class and the navy made it a national institution, it established the Gilbert and Sullivan partnership as the most successful in theatrical history, and it is a permanent part of the English comic repertory.

title: Patience; or, Bunthorne's Bride
description: First performed in 1881 and the definitive Victorian satire of the aesthetic movement: a village of love-sick maidens adores two rival poets.
plot_or_argument: The twenty lovesick maidens of Castle Bunthorne abandon their soldier lovers for the aesthetic poet Bunthorne and his rival Grosvenor; Patience, the simple milkmaid, is the only one immune to aesthetics, and the opera ends with the poets renouncing poetry for the simple life and the maidens returning to their redcoats.
principal_characters: Reginald Bunthorne; Archibald Grosvenor; Patience; Lady Jane; Lady Angela; Colonel Calverley; the Duke of Dunstable
historical_context: 1881: the aesthetic movement of the 1870s-80s, the Grosvenor Gallery, Oscar Wilde's early public image, and the vogue of the 'greenery-yallery' pose.
literary_significance: Patience is the definitive satire of the aesthetic movement and one of the most important documents of Victorian cultural history: Wilde's tour of America as part of the opera's promotion made him famous, the opera fixed the popular image of the aesthete for ever, and it is the funniest treatment of the art-for-art's-sake movement in English.

title: The Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu
description: First performed in 1885 and the most popular of the Savoy operas: a Japanese town where flirting is a capital offence and every problem is solved by a legal technicality.
plot_or_argument: Nanki-Poo, the Mikado's son, loves Yum-Yum, who is betrothed to the tailor Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner; Ko-Ko must produce an execution to satisfy the Mikado, and Nanki-Poo agrees to be beheaded after a month of marriage to Yum-Yum, but the discovery that the Mikado's son cannot be executed and the exaggerated report of an execution produce a legal crisis resolved by the Mikado's own arrival.
principal_characters: The Mikado; Nanki-Poo; Yum-Yum; Ko-Ko; Pooh-Bah; Pish-Tush; Katisha; Peep-Bo; Pitti-Sing
historical_context: 1885: the English fascination with Japan after the 1860s, the Gilbertian satire of English bureaucracy, and the Savoy theatre's spectacular production.
literary_significance: The Mikado is the most performed of all the Savoy operas and one of the most successful theatrical works ever written: its satire of bureaucracy and its comic logic made it a permanent institution in Britain, America and Australia, and its Japanese setting created a vogue that changed English decorative art.

title: The Gondoliers; or, The King of Barataria
description: First performed in 1889 and the last of the great Savoy operas: two Venetian gondoliers discover that one of them is the king of a foreign country.
plot_or_argument: Marco and Giuseppe Palmieri, gondoliers of Venice, learn that one of them is the kidnapped heir of Barataria and that both are married to the same woman; the arrival of the Grand Inquisitor and the discovery that the real king is the drummer boy Luiz resolves the plot, and the opera ends with the republican principles of the gondoliers restored.
principal_characters: Marco Palmieri; Giuseppe Palmieri; Gianetta; Tessa; the Duke of Plaza-Toro; the Duchess; Casilda; Luiz; Don Alhambra del Bolero
historical_context: 1889: the republican movement of the 1880s-90s, the Venetian setting of the Grand Tour, and the English debate on monarchy and democracy.
literary_significance: The Gondoliers is the last of the great Gilbert and Sullivan collaborations and their most politically radical opera: its argument for republican equality and its satire of the divine right of kings made it a landmark, and it is generally considered the most musically accomplished of the Savoy operas.

title: The Yeomen of the Guard; or, The Merryman and His Maid
description: First performed in 1888 and the darkest of the Savoy operas: a jester's unrequited love in the Tower of London under the Tudors.
plot_or_argument: Colonel Fairfax, condemned to death as a sorcerer, is secretly married to Elsie Maynard by the jester Jack Point; the marriage saves Fairfax when his reprieve arrives, but Elsie loves Fairfax and Point, who loves Elsie, is left at the end to fall senseless on the stage in one of the darkest endings in Victorian comic opera.
principal_characters: Jack Point; Elsie Maynard; Colonel Fairfax; Phoebe Meryll; Wilfred Shadbolt; Sergeant Meryll; Sir Richard Cholmondeley
literary_form: Comic opera (two acts) with tragic elements
historical_context: 1888: the Tower of London and the Tudor revival, the Victorian interest in the historical romance, and the Savoy opera's move toward the serious.
literary_significance: The Yeomen of the Guard is the most musically ambitious of the Savoy operas and its most emotionally serious: the character of Jack Point and the refusal of a happy ending made it a critical favourite, and it is the work in which Gilbert's comic and tragic gifts come closest to balance.

title: The Second Mrs Tanqueray
description: First performed in 1893 and the central English problem play of the 1890s: a woman with a past marries a respectable widower and is destroyed by the double standard.
plot_or_argument: Paula Tanqueray, formerly the mistress of several men, marries Aubrey Tanqueray, a widower, and tries to enter respectable society; her stepdaughter Ellean's engagement is broken off because of Paula's past, and Paula, realising that she can never be accepted, takes her own life, leaving Aubrey and Ellean to the conventional world.
principal_characters: Paula Tanqueray; Aubrey Tanqueray; Ellean Tanqueray; Sir George Orreyd; Mrs Cortelyon; Captain Ardale; Dr Wynne; Morse
historical_context: 1893: the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, the double standard in Victorian law, the New Woman debate, and the Lord Chamberlain's censorship of the stage.
literary_significance: The Second Mrs Tanqueray was the most discussed English play of the 1890s and the founding work of the English problem drama: its treatment of the woman with a past, its refusal of a comfortable ending and its exposure of the double standard made it the model for the serious English theatre, and it prepared the way for Shaw and the new drama.

title: Trelawny of the 'Wells'
description: First performed in 1898 and Pinero's warmest comedy: an actress of the old Sadler's Wells school tries to enter respectable society and returns to the stage.
plot_or_argument: Rose Trelawny, the leading lady of the theatre company at the Sadler's Wells in the 1860s, becomes engaged to Arthur Gower, a young gentleman, and tries to live with his family; she cannot bear the drawing room, returns to the theatre, and is finally reunited with Arthur when he becomes an actor himself.
principal_characters: Rose Trelawny; Arthur Gower; Sir William Gower; Vice-Chancellor Sir William; Miss Trafalgar Gower; Tom Wrench; Avonia Bunn; Mr Balfour
historical_context: 1898: the Victorian theatre of the 1860s, the passing of the old stock companies, the social stigma of the actress, and the new respectability of the stage.
literary_significance: Trelawny of the 'Wells' is the finest English theatrical comedy of the century and a loving memorial to the world of the old stock companies: its portrait of the Victorian stage made it a permanent classic, and it is the play in which Pinero's craftsmanship serves pure affection.

title: The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith
description: First performed in 1895 and the boldest of Pinero's problem plays: a freethinking woman who lives openly with a politician, and her return to the faith of her childhood.
plot_or_argument: Agnes Ebbsmith, a freethinker who has lived with the politician Lucas Cleeve, is confronted with his ambition to marry a rich woman; she destroys his career to save him, and then, in a final act of renunciation, takes up the Bible she had thrown into the fire and returns to the faith of her childhood.
principal_characters: Agnes Ebbsmith; Lucas Cleeve; Sir George Brodrick; Gertrude Thorpe; the Rev. Amos Winterfield; Sybil Cleeve
historical_context: 1895: the New Woman debate, the secularist and freethought movements, the 1895 moral panic after the Wilde trials, and the censorship of the stage.
literary_significance: The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith was one of the boldest English plays about free union and was attacked by the censors and the press: its portrait of a woman who chooses both intellectual freedom and religious faith made it one of the most interesting problem plays of the decade, and it is the finest of Pinero's serious works after The Second Mrs Tanqueray.

title: The Magistrate
description: First performed in 1885 and the most durable English farce of the century: a respectable magistrate is arrested in his own court after a night of mistaken identity.
plot_or_argument: Mr Posket, a London police magistrate, takes his family to a hotel, where his wife's age is misreported and his stepson's gambling leads to a series of mistaken identities; the next morning Posket finds himself on the bench trying his own case, in a farce of escalating confusion resolved only by the discovery that everyone is related.
principal_characters: Mr Posket; Agatha Posket; Cis Farringdon; Charlotte Verrinder; Colonel Lukyn; Captain Horace Vale; Mr Bullamy
historical_context: 1885: the Victorian police court, the late-Victorian hotel, the farce tradition of the Court Theatre, and the fashion for the 'well-made' comedy of situation.
literary_significance: The Magistrate is the finest English farce of the century and one of the most durable comedies in the language: its construction and its dialogue made it the model for the English stage farce, and it established Pinero as the leading comic craftsman of the 1880s.

title: The Gay Lord Quex
description: First performed in 1899 and Pinero's most elegant comedy of manners: a reformed rake is tested by the manicurist who knows his past.
plot_or_argument: Lord Quex, a reformed roué of fifty, is engaged to Muriel Eden, a young woman of strict principles; Sophy Fullgarney, his former mistress and now a fashionable manicurist, sets out to expose him, and the play ends with Sophy's generosity saving the marriage and Quex's real reformation confirmed.
principal_characters: Lord Quex; Muriel Eden; Sophy Fullgarney; Sir Chichester Frayne; Mrs Eden; Jack Eden; the Duchess of Strood
historical_context: 1899: the fashion for the manicure and the beauty parlour, the Victorian double standard, and the West End theatre of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Gay Lord Quex is Pinero's wittiest comedy of manners and one of the most accomplished English plays of the 1890s: its portrait of the reformed rake and the professional woman made it a success, and it is the play in which Pinero's craftsmanship and his social observation are most perfectly united.

title: The Silver King
description: First performed in 1882 and the most successful English melodrama of the decade: a ruined gentleman is accused of murder and redeemed by the love of a good woman.
plot_or_argument: Wilfred Denver, a spendthrift, is drunkenly present at a murder and believes himself the killer; he flees to America, becomes a successful prospector, and returns in disguise to clear his name and save his wife and children, in a melodrama of gambling, drink, escape and providential rescue.
principal_characters: Wilfred Denver; Nellie Denver; Geoffrey Ware; Corkett; Jaikes; Skinner; Brierly
historical_context: 1882: the English melodrama of the 1880s, the gold rush of the American West, the temperance movement, and the Princess's Theatre productions of Wilson Barrett.
literary_significance: The Silver King was the most successful English melodrama of its decade and one of the finest examples of the form: its combination of moral seriousness and spectacular stagecraft made it a model for the serious melodrama, and it established Jones as the leading young dramatist of the 1880s.

title: Saints and Sinners
description: First performed in 1884 and the first English play to put a Nonconformist minister on the stage: a clergyman's daughter is seduced and the town's piety is exposed.
plot_or_argument: Jacob Fletcher, a popular Dissenting minister, is confronted with the ruin of his daughter Letty by the son of a local landowner; the play exposes the hypocrisy of the congregation, the cruelty of the village's moral code, and the minister's own failure of sympathy, and ends with Letty dead and the father broken.
historical_context: 1884: the Nonconformist conscience of the English provinces, the Victorian double standard, and the debate on the morality of the stage.
literary_significance: Saints and Sinners was the first English play to treat Dissent and provincial respectability seriously and one of the founding works of the English problem drama: it shocked the critics and the clergy, it made the case for a serious drama of contemporary life, and it preceded Pinero's problem plays by a decade.

title: The Middleman
description: First performed in 1889 and the first English play about industrial capital: a manufacturer and his son-in-law, the middleman, in conflict over a new process.
plot_or_argument: Cyrus Blenkarn, a self-made manufacturer, has invented a process that will ruin his own trade; his son-in-law Chandler, the middleman, fights him for control of the works, and the play ends with Blenkarn's death and the ruin of the family, in a drama of industrial conflict and the ethics of capital.
historical_context: 1889: the industrial depression of the 1880s, the new capitalism of the Midlands, the labour movement of the 1880s, and the fashion for the drama of ideas after Ibsen.
literary_significance: The Middleman was the first English play to put industrial capitalism on the stage and one of the earliest English dramas of ideas: its portrait of the manufacturer and its argument about the ethics of wealth made it a landmark, and it is a key document of the English theatre's turn to social questions.

title: Mrs Dane's Defence
description: First performed in 1900 and the finest English problem play before Shaw: a woman with a past is cross-examined before the man she is to marry.
plot_or_argument: Mrs Dane, a widow engaged to a young man of good family, is confronted with her former life by Sir Daniel Carteret, a barrister and the young man's guardian; the third act is a cross-examination in which she is trapped into confessing, and the play ends with her leaving the house and the family's respectability preserved at the cost of their humanity.
principal_characters: Mrs Dane; Sir Daniel Carteret; Lionel Carteret; Lady Eastney; Mr Risby; Mrs Bulsom-Porter; Fendick
historical_context: 1900: the Victorian double standard, the law of divorce, the censorship of the stage, and the vogue of the problem play at the end of the century.
literary_significance: Mrs Dane's Defence is the most accomplished English problem play of the period and one of the finest in the language: its third act is the strongest scene of cross-examination written for the English stage, and it is the play in which the Victorian drama of the fallen woman reached its highest point.

title: The Case of Rebellious Susan
description: First performed in 1894 and the wittiest English comedy on the double standard: a wife retaliates against her husband's infidelity and finds the retaliation harder than the injury.
plot_or_argument: Lady Susan Harabin, whose husband has been unfaithful, takes a young admirer to Cairo as a deliberate counter-scandal; the comedy follows her husband's fury, her own disillusion, and the worldly-wise intervention of her older friend Sir Richard, who arranges a reconciliation in which nobody is allowed to be honest.
principal_characters: Lady Susan Harabin; Sir Richard Kato; Lucius Harabin; Elaine Shrimpton; Lady Darlington; the Rev. Mr Brabazon
historical_context: 1894: the New Woman debate, the divorce law and the double standard, the English colony in Cairo, and the West End theatre of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Case of Rebellious Susan is the most intelligent English comedy on the double standard of the 1890s: its wit and its refusal of either sentimentality or moralising made it the model for the modern comedy of manners, and it is the best of Jones's social plays.

title: In Hospital
description: Published in Poems (1898/1900) and the first English poetic sequence about surgery and hospital life: the poems written after Henley's amputation at the Edinburgh Infirmary.
plot_or_argument: The sequence follows the poet through the ward: the clinical examinations, the operations, the ether, the sleepless nights, the dying patient in the next bed, the nurses, the visitors and the slow return of the sense of the body, in poems of exact physical detail and hard, unsentimental rhythm.
historical_context: 1873-75: the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary and Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery, the Victorian hospital ward, and the poetic realism of the 1870s.
literary_significance: In Hospital is a landmark of English poetry about illness and the body: it was the first sustained English poem to treat surgery and hospital life with clinical realism, and its influence on the war poetry of the twentieth century and on modern poetry of illness is direct and acknowledged.

title: 'Invictus'
description: Written in 1875 and published in 1888: the most quoted English poem of heroic defiance, the stoic's answer to fate.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, in the darkness of a fate that has beaten him, thanks whatever gods may be for his unconquerable soul; under the bludgeonings of chance his head is bloody but unbowed, and he declares himself the master of his fate and the captain of his soul.
historical_context: 1875: the Victorian crisis of faith, the stoicism of the age of Darwin, and Henley's own experience of illness and amputation.
literary_significance: 'Invictus' is one of the most quoted poems in English and the central Victorian poem of stoic defiance: it gave the language its great statement of self-mastery, it has been cited by statesmen and prisoners across the world, and it is the poem by which Henley is permanently known.

title: Hawthorn and Lavender, with Other Verses
description: Published in 1901 and Henley's last collection: love poems, hospital memories and the imperial songs of his final years.
plot_or_argument: The title sequence follows a love affair through the seasons, with the hawthorn of spring and the lavender of summer standing for the phases of passion; the other poems return to the hospital, to the city, and to the imperial themes of the 1890s.
historical_context: 1898-1901: the imperial enthusiasm of the Boer War, the London literary world of the National Observer, and Henley's last illness.
literary_significance: Hawthorn and Lavender is Henley's most sustained love sequence and the finest of his later work: it shows the lyric gift that his admirers valued above the imperial rhetoric, and it is the collection in which his two themes — the body and desire — are most completely joined.

title: The Testament of Beauty
description: Published in 1929 and Bridges's last and most ambitious poem: a philosophy of beauty, evolution and the mind of man in a new metre.
plot_or_argument: The poem argues through a series of meditations — on the beauty of the natural world, on the evolution of consciousness, on the difference between the animal and the human, on love, on the State and on the future of civilisation — that beauty is the manifestation of an ordering power in things and that man's task is to cooperate with it.
historical_context: 1929: the aftermath of the First World War, the modernism of Eliot and Pound, the new biology, and the public hunger for a philosophy of order.
literary_significance: The Testament of Beauty was a best-seller and a public event in 1929 and the last great English philosophical poem: its new metre and its argument for a spiritual reading of evolution made it a landmark of the interwar period, and it is the summation of Bridges's lifelong thinking about beauty and order.

title: Shorter Poems
description: Published in 1890 and Bridges's finest collection of lyrics: love poems, nature poems and songs of a classical perfection.
plot_or_argument: The collection gathers the lyrics of twenty years — the sonnets of The Growth of Love, the songs of the English countryside, the poems on music and on the death of friends — in forms of exquisite finish and classical restraint.
historical_context: 1873-90: the Oxford of Pater and Hopkins, the English country house, and the reaction against the rhetoric of Tennyson and Swinburne.
literary_significance: Shorter Poems is the finest English lyric collection of its decade and the model of classical restraint in Victorian verse: its technical perfection made Bridges the poet's poet of his generation, and it contains some of the most perfect short poems in the language.

title: The Growth of Love
description: Published in 1876 and Bridges's first major work: a sonnet sequence on the growth of love in the mind of a young man.
plot_or_argument: The sequence traces the awakening and the deepening of love in a young man's consciousness, through doubt, absence and the fear of loss, to a settled and mature devotion in which the beloved is seen as the visible form of a universal beauty.
historical_context: 1876: the Victorian sonnet revival after Rossetti and Meredith, the Oxford of the 1870s, and the Platonic tradition of English love poetry.
literary_significance: The Growth of Love is one of the finest English sonnet sequences after Meredith and Rossetti: its restraint and its Platonic seriousness made it a critical favourite, and it established Bridges as the most technically accomplished of the younger Victorian poets.

title: Admirals All and Other Verses
description: Published in 1897 and the most popular imperial poetry collection of the decade: naval ballads, school songs and the poems of the imperial creed.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Vitaï Lampada', 'Drake's Drum', 'The Fighting Temeraire' and 'Admirals All', in which the navy, the public school and the empire are celebrated in ballads with strong refrains and simple, memorable measures.
historical_context: 1896-97: the Diamond Jubilee of 1897, the naval arms race with Germany, the public school cult of games, and the imperial enthusiasm of the 1890s.
literary_significance: Admirals All was the best-selling poetry collection of 1897 and the central text of the imperial ideal in verse: 'Vitaï Lampada' became the most quoted poem of the public school ethos, and the collection is the essential document of imperial sentiment at its height.
